items.title: Inference Opens: Reasoning From Marks Already Seen

items.zh: 比量者，謂與思擇俱，已思應思所有境思。此復五種。一、相比量，二、體比量，三、業比量，四、法比量，五、因果比量。
items.en: Inference: it refers to whatever object, joined with discerning deliberation, has already been deliberated on or is yet to be deliberated on. It again has five kinds: first, inference from characteristic marks; second, inference from essence; third, inference from function; fourth, inference from association; and fifth, inference from cause and effect.

items.zh: 相比量者，謂隨所有相狀相屬，或由現在，或先所見，推度境界。如見幢故，比知有車；由見烟故，比知有火。如是以王比國；以夫比妻；以角犎等，比知有牛；以膚細軟、髮黑、輕躁、容色妍美，比知少年；以面皺髮白等相，比知是老；以執持自相，比知道俗；以樂觀聖者、樂聞正法、遠離慳貪，比知正信；以善思所思、善說所說、善作所作，比知聰叡；以慈悲、愛語、勇猛、樂施、能善解釋甚深義趣，比知菩薩；以掉動、輕轉、嬉戲、歌笑等事，比未離欲；以諸威儀恒常寂靜，比知離欲；以具如來微妙相好、智慧、寂靜、正行、神通，比知如來、應、等正覺具一切智，
items.en: Inference from characteristic marks: it means, following some characteristic mark bound up with a thing, whether seen now or seen before, reasoning one's way to the object itself. As seeing a banner, one infers there is a chariot; seeing smoke, one infers there is fire... By what someone holds and carries, one infers whether they are a renunciant or a layperson; by delight in seeing the noble, delight in hearing the true Dharma, and freedom from stinginess, one infers genuine faith... By possessing the Tathāgata's sublime marks, wisdom, tranquility, right conduct, and supernormal powers, one infers a Tathāgata, worthy of offerings, a perfectly awakened one possessed of all-knowing wisdom.

items.zh: 以於老時，見彼幼年所有相狀，比知是彼。如是等類，名相比量。
items.en: By seeing, in someone's old age, the traces of the features they had in youth, one infers this is the same person. Things of this kind are called inference from characteristic marks.

items.title: Inference Complete: From Essence, Function, Association, and Cause to Effect

items.zh: 體比量者，謂現見彼自體性故，比類彼物不現見體；或現見彼一分自體，比類餘分。如以現在比類過去，或以過去比類未來，或以現在近事比遠，或以現在比於未來。又如飲食、衣服、嚴具、車乘等事，觀見一分得失之相，比知一切。又以一分成熟，比餘熟分。如是等類，名體比量。
items.en: Inference from essence: seeing directly some thing's own nature, one infers the nature of that same thing where it is not directly seen; or seeing directly one part of its nature, one infers the remaining parts. As inferring the past from the present, or the future from the past... Or again, as with food, clothing, ornaments, and vehicles: observing in one instance a mark of gain or loss, one infers the same of all; or from one part being ripe, one infers the rest is ripe as well. Things of this kind are called inference from essence.

items.zh: 業比量者，謂以作用比業所依。如見遠物無有動搖，鳥居其上，由是等事比知是杌；若有動搖等事，比知是人。廣跡住處，比知是象；曳身行處，比知是蛇。若聞嘶聲，比知是馬；若聞哮吼，比知師子；若聞咆勃，比知牛王。見比於眼，聞比於耳，嗅比於鼻，甞比於舌，觸比於身，識比於意。水中見礙，比知有地；若見是處草木滋潤、莖葉青翠，比知有水；若見熱灰，比知有火；叢林掉動，比知有風。瞑目執杖，進止問他，蹎蹶失路，如是等事比知是盲；高聲側聽，比知是聾。正信、聰叡、離欲、未離欲、菩薩、如來，如是等類以業比度，如前應知。
items.en: Inference from function: it means inferring what an activity depends on from the activity itself. As seeing a distant object entirely without movement, with a bird perched upon it, one infers from this that it is a dead stump; but where there is movement, one infers it is a person... The act of seeing implies an eye; hearing implies an ear; smelling implies a nose; tasting implies a tongue; touching implies a body; cognizing implies a mind... Seeing hot ash, one infers there was fire; a grove swaying, one infers there is wind... Inference of this kind, by function, should be understood as before.

items.zh: 法比量者，謂以相隣相屬之法，比餘相隣相屬之法。如屬無常，比知有苦；以屬苦故，比空、無我。以屬生故，比有老法；以屬老故，比有死法。以屬有色、有見、有對，比有方所及有形質。屬有漏故，比知有苦；屬無漏故，比知無苦。屬有為故，比知生住異滅之法；屬無為故，比知無生住異滅法。如是等類，名法比量。
items.en: Inference from association: it means inferring, from a phenomenon adjacent in meaning to or linked with another, some further phenomenon likewise adjacent or linked. As what belongs to impermanence, one infers belongs to suffering; what belongs to suffering, one infers is empty and without self. What belongs to birth, one infers has the nature of ageing; what belongs to ageing, one infers has the nature of death... Things of this kind are called inference from association.

items.zh: 因果比量者，謂以因果展轉相比。如見有行，比至餘方；見至餘方，比先有行。若見有人如法事王，比知當獲廣大祿位；見大祿位，比知先已如法事王。若見有人備善作業，比知必當獲大財富；見大財富，比知先已備善作業。見先修習善行惡行，比當興衰；見有興衰，比先造作善行惡行。見豐飲食，比知飽滿；見有飽滿，比豐飲食。若見有人食不平等，比當有病；現見有病，比知是人食不平等。見有靜慮，比知離欲；見離欲者，比有靜慮。若見修道，比知當獲沙門果證；若見有獲沙門果證，比知修道。如是等類，當知總名因果比量。是名比量。
items.en: Inference from cause and effect: it means inferring, cause and effect turning upon each other, from one to the other. As seeing someone walking, one infers they will arrive elsewhere; seeing they have arrived elsewhere, one infers they were walking before... Seeing meditative concentration, one infers freedom from desire; seeing one free of desire, one infers meditative concentration. Seeing one cultivate the path, one infers they will attain the fruit of a renunciant; seeing one who has attained that fruit, one infers they cultivated the path. Things of this kind should be known, all together, as inference from cause and effect. This is called inference.

blocks.text: Today's reading explains **inference** (比量, *anumāna*), the second means of valid knowledge, in five kinds. The examples are drawn from everyday life, and our teachers add their own. As you read, notice how much of what you "know" each day is inference.

Inference concerns objects "already deliberated or yet to be deliberated". Master Cháng Bǎi: reflecting on present or past objects is the first; on objects not yet present, the second. Inference reasons "from marks already seen" to what is not seen.

From a sign one infers what it signifies: smoke to fire, a banner to a chariot, a crowd to an event. The treatise also gives "inferring the wife from the husband". Master Cháng Bǎi: a neatly dressed husband suggests a capable wife; a dishevelled one, that she is lazy or very busy. He adds an example of his own: an old man takes out a photograph of a child; though he says nothing, one infers it is himself.
From part of a thing's nature one infers the rest: from one grain, that the pot of rice is cooked; from the present, the past.
From what a thing does, one infers what it is: from movement in the grass, a snake; from a footprint, an elephant.

From things "adjacent and connected": Master Cháng Bǎi distinguishes the two. Adjacent things share part of a meaning, like impermanence, suffering, and non-self; connected things always go together. From impermanence one infers suffering; from suffering, non-self (Day 89's order).

From a cause one infers its effect, and from an effect its cause, "in turn". Venerable Miào Jìng: "I compare with you, you compare with me": the inference runs both ways. From proper conduct one infers prosperity; from prosperity, past good conduct.

Much of the Buddhist path is learned by inference before it is known by perception. We infer karma from its results, impermanence from change, and the value of practice from the lives of practitioners. Inference is not second-rate knowledge; it is how a student becomes a practitioner. But the treatise ranks it after perception, because the aim is to see directly what was first inferred. Tomorrow: the third means, scriptural authority.

quiz.q: Inference concerns objects "already or yet to be deliberated." How does Master Cháng Bǎi divide the two?
options: reflecting on present or past objects is "already"; on objects not yet present is "yet to be"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Reflecting on and discriminating present or past objects is 'already deliberated'; on objects not yet present is 'yet to be deliberated.'" Venerable Miào Jìng: inference reasons from the known to the unknown.

quiz.q: Among inferences from marks is "inferring the wife from the husband" (elided in f15). What example does Master Cháng Bǎi give?
options: a rich husband means a rich wife
a tall husband, a tall wife
a neatly dressed husband shows a capable wife; a disheveled one suggests she is lazy or very busy
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: seeing the husband always neatly dressed, one knows the wife is capable; if his clothes are a mess, one infers she is lazy — or very busy. Venerable Miào Jìng mentions the inference only in general.

quiz.q: The English renders 如是等類 as "Discourse of this kind." What's wrong, and how does Master Cháng Bǎi explain inferring youth from old age?
options: there is no "discourse" in the original — it means "cases of this kind"; Cháng Bǎi's example is an old man's childhood photo, an inference from what was seen before
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: seeing an old man take out a childhood photo, though he doesn't say it's him, one infers from the features that it is. 如是等類 means "cases of this kind," unrelated to "discourse."

quiz.q: Inference from association uses things "adjacent and connected." How do the lectures distinguish 相鄰 and 相屬, and what does the note do?
options: adjacency is partial overlap of meaning, like impermanence, suffering, selflessness; connection is one thing producing the next, like birth, ageing, death; the note merges both as necessary implication
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: these dharmas differ but their meanings are adjacent — sharing something, yet only partly, hence "adjacent." Venerable Miào Jìng likewise distinguishes the two. The note and the English flatten the distinction.

quiz.q: Inference from cause and effect works "in turn." How does Venerable Miào Jìng define 展轉?
options: I compare to you and you to me — cause to effect and effect to cause; one-way is not 展轉
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "I compare with you, you compare with me — that is 'in turn.' If only cause is compared to effect and not effect to cause, it can't be called 'in turn.'" The treatise's examples run both ways.
